metaDescription: Six inkjet and ink tank printers for cardstock, invitations and craft projects, with paper path, rear feed, pigment ink and wide-format advice.
expertTake: The Epson EcoTank Photo ET-8550 is the best overall pick for cardstock because it takes wide sheets and uses six inks with a gentle feed. The Canon PIXMA TS6520 is the value pick for occasional invitations on standard sizes. If you print heavy stock only once or twice a year, a local print shop beats owning any of these.
introParagraphs: Cardstock is thicker and stiffer than office paper, so it resists the sharp turns a normal printer paper path puts it through. A printer that handles it well either has a rear or straight feed, or a robust roller system that grips stiff sheets without skewing them.

Buyers print cardstock for invitations, greeting cards, labels, scrapbook pages and crafts, and each of those cares about different things: color fidelity, borderless edges, sheet size or the ink staying put on a coated surface. Knowing which job you do most narrows the field quickly.

products.name: Epson EcoTank Photo ET-8550 Wide-Format 6-Color Tank Printer
products.description:
The ET-8550 pairs a six-color ink tank system with wide-format output, so it can print 13 by 19 inch sheets as well as standard sizes. The extra colors give smoother gradients on card faces, which matters when you print a photo or a color wash on an invitation.

Its rear and front paper paths for thicker media are the reason it tops this list, since cardstock bends less on the rear route than around a curved internal path. Against the XP-15000, it replaces cartridges with ink bottles, so running cost per card is far lower for a craft hobbyist printing in volume.

Ownership means filling the tanks carefully and printing regularly so the printhead stays clear. It is a large machine with a big footprint, so measure shelf space first. Test your cardstock on a cheap sheet, because every printer sets its thickness limit in the manual and exceeding it is the fastest way to a jam. Owners who print invitations for a wedding or a school event should also run a short test batch of five or six cards before committing, since color on the screen and color on coated card rarely match on the first pass. The wide body also means you should leave clearance behind it for the rear feed to work, and a cramped shelf is the usual reason people complain about the feed route.
products.bestFor: Craft and card makers who print photos, invitations and large sheets.
pros: Six inks give smoother color gradients
Wide format up to 13 by 19 inches
Refillable tanks keep running cost low
cons: Large and heavy for a desk
Needs regular use to avoid clogging
Highest entry cost in the group

products.name: Epson Expression Photo HD XP-15000 Wide-Format 6-Color Printer
products.description:
The XP-15000 is a wide-format cartridge printer with six Claria Photo HD inks, including red and gray, to widen the color range and improve black and white. For photo cards on coated cardstock it gives the richest result in this list.

The tradeoff is running cost. Cartridges are pricier per page than the bottle system in the ET-8550, so it suits someone printing a modest number of special pieces rather than a stack every week. The Epson design also requires genuine cartridges, which limits cheaper alternatives.

Owners get the best results when they print regularly and keep the printer in a stable room, since cartridge printheads can dry. Feed cardstock one sheet at a time through the route the manual suggests, and let ink dry before stacking, because coated card holds wet ink longer than plain paper. If you print only photo cards a few times a year, weigh whether the cartridge cost and the drying risk justify the machine over an online card service, because the XP-15000 earns its place only when you print often enough to keep the printhead in good shape. Genuine cartridge pricing also adds up across six colors, so check each cartridge before you commit to a large project.
products.bestFor: A photographer or card maker who wants top color and wide sheets.
pros: Six inks including red and gray
Strong photo and black and white quality

products.name: Epson EcoTank ET-15000 Wireless Wide-Format Supertank Printer
products.description:
The ET-15000 is a wide-format ink tank all-in-one that prints large pages without the cartridge costs of the XP-15000. It is aimed at someone who prints big sheets, such as posters, flyers or oversized cards, and wants a low cost per page.

Compared with the ET-8550, it has fewer colors, so photo gradients are less smooth, but text and graphics on card stock are sharp. If the cardstock is mostly text, borders and flat color, this is the more economical choice.

It is big, so give it a table, and plan on weekly printing to keep nozzles open. Keep bottles upright and stored cool, and check the manual for the maximum media weight before buying a ream of heavy stock. A wide-format body also changes how you store supplies: sheets of 13 by 19 inch card need a flat box or a drawer, because curled stock is the leading cause of crooked feeding on any large printer. If your projects are mostly posters and flyers, the ET-15000 gives you the format without paying for the photo-grade inks of the ET-8550.
products.bestFor: People printing large flyers and cards in volume without photo-grade color.
pros: Wide format at low ink cost
Good text and graphics on card

products.name: Canon MegaTank G3270 Wireless All-in-One Refillable Tank Printer
products.description:
The G3270 uses refillable tanks and Canon rates one set of inks at up to 6,000 black and 7,700 color pages. For standard letter-size cardstock jobs such as greeting cards and flash cards, the cost per sheet is very low.

It is a compact desktop printer, so it avoids the bulk of the wide-format Epsons, though it cannot print oversize sheets. Compared with the Epson ET-4800, it drops the fax and the document feeder and wins on rated yield.

Owners should fill tanks from the bottles slowly and print regularly. Check the thickest media the rear or front tray will accept, since thick cardstock exceeding the limit can skew and jam. The machine suits a kitchen table or a craft desk because the tanks are built into the body, so there is no separate ink tower to find room for. It will not handle posters, but for the flash cards, place cards and recipe cards most households make, the format limit rarely matters. Keep a spare ink set in a cool cupboard so a long project never stalls on an empty tank.
products.bestFor: Letter-size card projects at a low running cost.
pros: Low cost per page with tank yield

products.badge: Best for Home Office Plus Cards
products.name: Epson EcoTank ET-4800 Wireless Supertank All-in-One with Fax
products.description:
The ET-4800 is an ink tank all-in-one with fax, built for a home office that also prints the odd card or label. Its Micro Piezo heat-free printhead is the Epson approach that keeps ink liquid without a thermal element.

Against the Canon G3270, it adds fax and a feeder-oriented office feature set, so it makes more sense if cardstock is a side job. It is not designed for wide sheets, and standard cardstock is the main fit.

Plan for the usual tank routine and keep ink bottles stored upright. Load cardstock singly and check the media limit in the manual, since thicker paper may require a particular tray.
products.bestFor: A home office that prints cards occasionally and needs fax and scanning.
pros: Fax, scan and copy in one body

products.name: Canon PIXMA TS6520 Wireless Color Inkjet All-in-One
products.description:
The TS6520 is a compact cartridge inkjet with a two-cartridge system and a small OLED display. It is the entry point for someone who prints a few cards or invitations a year and does not want to deal with tanks.

The compromise is running cost and color range. Two cartridges cannot match six-ink photo printers, and cartridge refills cost more per page than tank bottles, so it is a poor fit for volume.

For ownership, print a page every couple of weeks so the cartridges do not dry, and feed cardstock one sheet at a time. It fits a shelf easily, which helps in a small craft space.
products.bestFor: Occasional card and invitation printing on standard sizes.
cons: Cartridge ink costs more per page

buyingCriteria.explanation: Cardstock jams when it is bent around a tight curve, so a rear or front straight path is the single most useful feature. The Epson ET-8550 includes a route for thicker media, while a compact machine like the Canon TS6520 relies on standard trays. Always check the printer's listed maximum media weight and load one sheet at a time.

Cardstock may be coated or uncoated, and ink behaves differently on each. Uncoated stock soaks up dye ink and can look dull, while coated stock holds ink on the surface and takes longer to dry. Printers like the Epson XP-15000 use Claria photo inks suited to coated media, while text heavy jobs on matte card do well on most tank printers.

Photo cards benefit from extra inks such as the red and gray in the XP-15000 and the six-color ET-8550, which smooth gradients and improve black. A two-cartridge printer such as the Canon TS6520 is fine for text and flat color. Pay for more colors only if you print photographs.

Most card projects are letter size, but posters, large invitations and scrapbook pages need wide sheets. The ET-8550, XP-15000 and ET-15000 print up to 13 by 19 inches. Smaller machines such as the Canon MegaTank G3270 are far easier to place on a desk.

Tank printers lower cost per card substantially. The Canon G3270 is rated up to 6,000 black and 7,700 color pages per set, while cartridge printers like the TS6520 cost more per page. For craft volume, the tank route usually pays back quickly.

Heavy ink coverage on thick card can stay wet and smudge when stacked. Print one at a time, let each dry, and use the printer's heavy paper setting if it has one. Pigment inks resist smear better than dye once dry.

specDecoder.meaning: Printing to the edge of the sheet without a white margin. It needs the printer to spray slightly past the paper edge.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Epson XP-15000 and ET-8550 print borderless on wide sheets, and many cheaper models limit borderless to certain sizes.

specDecoder.meaning: A tray at the back that feeds paper straight into the path. It avoids the tight curve of a front tray.
specDecoder.watchFor: The ET-8550 and similar models offer routes for thick media, so verify the feed type before buying.

specDecoder.meaning: The rated number of pages from a set of ink at standard coverage. Heavy card coverage uses more ink than the rating implies.
specDecoder.watchFor: The G3270 lists up to 6,000 black and 7,700 color pages, but dense card art will use more.

specDecoder.meaning: The number of separate inks. More colors give smoother gradients and a wider gamut.
specDecoder.watchFor: The XP-15000 uses six Claria inks including red and gray, while the TS6520 uses two cartridges.

specDecoder.meaning: Support for paper larger than letter, such as 13 by 19 inches.
specDecoder.watchFor: The ET-15000 and ET-8550 take wide sheets, and a compact machine does not. Wide models also need more bench space and a wider rear clearance, so measure before ordering and remember that large sheets are costlier to stock and to store flat.

howWeEvaluated.title: Paper handling
howWeEvaluated.description: We evaluated the likelihood of a clean feed for stiff sheets based on listed paper paths and media options. Rear feed machines scored higher, and compact curved paths lower. We cross-checked against owner feedback patterns on jams.

howWeEvaluated.title: Color capability
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared ink counts, such as the six inks of the ET-8550 against the two cartridges in the TS6520. More inks scored higher for photo cards and flat color suits any model. This follows the spec sheet.

howWeEvaluated.title: Running cost
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed yield and cartridge versus tank ink. The Canon G3270 at up to 6,000 black pages scored high, and cartridge models scored lower. Heavy card coverage was assumed to use more ink.

howWeEvaluated.title: Format flexibility
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered sheet size. The ET-15000, ET-8550 and XP-15000 print up to 13 by 19 inches, while compact models stop at letter. The flexibility scored higher for large format jobs.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership effort
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at refilling, nozzle care and size. Tank printers need careful filling and regular use, and cartridge models dry if idle. A small footprint scored higher for tight spaces.

rows: Wide format at low ink cost

cards.label: Cartridge
cards.text: The Canon TS6520 and Epson XP-15000 are cheap or photo-focused at purchase, but each card costs more in ink. They suit low volume.

cards.label: Ink tank
cards.text: The Epson ET-8550, ET-15000, ET-4800 and Canon G3270 cost more upfront and far less per sheet. They suit craft volume.

howToChoose.note: Low volume goes to cartridge, regular crafting goes to tanks.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Look for a straight paper path, borderless printing, good color and a media weight limit that covers your stock. Test one sheet and let it dry before running more.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Epson ET-8550 is the best match, with six inks and a thick-media route. The Canon TS6520 handles simple text invitations at lower cost.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: Pay extra if you print photo cards or large sheets weekly, which points to the Epson ET-8550 or ET-15000.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Save if you print a few cards a year, where the Canon TS6520 or G3270 is enough.

maintenance.why: Idle nozzles dry out and streak cards. A quick check keeps color clean.
Thickness limits vary. A test sheet avoids a jam and wasted card.
Coated card leaves residue that reduces grip. A damp lint-free cloth restores feeding.
Humid or curled cardstock jams. Keep it sealed in its original wrapper.
Spilled ink stains cards and the machine. Fill slowly and keep bottles upright.

faq.q: What printer is best for cardstock?
faq.a: A printer with a rear or straight feed handles stiff sheets best. The Epson ET-8550 leads this list for thick media and color, and the Canon G3270 is a lower cost tank option.

faq.q: Can any inkjet print on cardstock?
faq.a: Many can, up to a thickness limit listed in the manual. Exceeding the limit causes jams and skewed prints, so check the maximum media weight first.

faq.q: Is a tank printer worth it for cards?
faq.a: If you print regularly, yes. The Canon G3270 is rated up to 6,000 black pages per set, so card costs are low, though tanks need regular use.
Only for photo cards and smooth gradients. The XP-15000 and ET-8550 use six inks, while the TS6520 is fine for text and flat color.
Dye ink on coated stock stays wet longer. Print one sheet at a time and allow drying before stacking.

Only on wide-format models. The ET-8550, XP-15000 and ET-15000 print up to 13 by 19 inches, while compact printers stop at letter size. If you only ever print letter-size cards, skip the wide models entirely and put the savings toward good stock and spare ink.
